title: The Almoner

where.detail: standing at his cot in the infirmary hall, the almoner on the next cot, Hollis in a carried chair at its foot

time: dawn, the morning after the lid came off
last_beat: Behind them, at the far end of the row, the thin novice was on his knees on the flags with his ear to the floor, listening, and when he saw the Captain looking he got up, and dusted his knees, and went on with his bread.

people.did: Told the thin novice at the night bell and the Prior at the dawn bell, on his own leg with his fingertips wrapped; heard the almoner's confession; stopped Hollis with his full name and an order, the first since the ford; told the almoner to stay in the hall, keep the stores key and give it to nobody.
people.now: Standing at his cot with the ends of his right-hand fingers wrapped in Maelis's linen, the almoner on the next cot under his eye and the stores key still on the man's belt. The next letter from Calden comes up with the carter.

facts.fact: He told the Prior everything in the chapel at the dawn bell, after the far cots' keeper, and said the order of telling was Hollis's asking.
facts.evidence: He told her it had been Hollis's asking that the keepers came first, because it was.

facts.fact: He knows there is a second way down to the undercroft: the old wine stair from the stores, opened by the stores key, which comes out behind a pillar at the kitchen end of the hall below.
facts.evidence: So there were two ways down.

facts.fact: He stopped Hollis with his full name and the voice from the ford, which he had not used since the water, and ordered him to sit.
facts.evidence: It came out of Darrow in the voice from the ford, the one that had put the Ninth into a line it did not want to hold.

facts.fact: He ordered the almoner to stay in the hall, eat, and keep the stores key on him, giving it to nobody, not the Prior, not Darrow himself.
facts.evidence: You'll keep the stores key on you and you'll give it to nobody, not the Prior, not me.

facts.fact: He stood up without remembering getting up, and the knee held.
facts.evidence: He did not remember getting up. The knee held.

people.did: Heard it all in the chapel before the lamps were lit, said once that she had counted the nights between, two, and that she says every name under the roof every night and will go on saying all of them; asked nothing.
people.now: In the chapel at dawn, the first lamp lit. She knows what is under the House and has said her one thing about where she came in the order of telling.

facts.fact: She counted the nights between his promise at the stair head and his telling: two.
facts.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.

facts.fact: She says every name under the roof in the chapel every night, has not had to stop saying one since he came, and will go on saying all of them.
facts.evidence: I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came. I shall go on saying all of them.

people.did: Had himself carried in a poled chair at the end of the dawn bell with the almoner walking in front of it, having had the man's confession at the third bell; leaned at him with his whole weight when the man said mercy; stopped at his full name and sat back at the Captain's order.
people.now: In the carried chair at the foot of Darrow's cot, the lad's blanket folded on his knee, his hands off the poles. He said Captain.

facts.fact: He had the almoner's confession at the third bell of the night and brought him to the Captain at dawn.
facts.evidence: Tell the Captain what you told me at the third bell.

facts.fact: He stopped at his full name and the order to sit, and said Captain.
facts.evidence: "Captain," he said.

people.did: Was brought to the Captain shaking, and confessed: the stores key opens the old wine stair down to the undercroft; a clerk in grey at the winch-house, who wrote and never knelt, gave him two wrapped things before the snow and called them a mercy for the wounded, with his sister's letter under his hand; he set the first under the hall by the wine stair and was sick on the stair; the second was still in his satchel, and he gave it to Maelis.
people.now: On the cot next to Darrow's, ordered to stay in the hall where the Captain can see him, to eat, and to keep the stores key and give it to nobody. The next letter from Calden comes with the carter.

facts.fact: The stores key opens the old stair door where the wine was laid, below the kitchen end; the stair comes out in the undercroft hall behind a pillar at the kitchen end; he never used the flour door.
facts.evidence: It comes out in the hall below, at the kitchen end, behind a pillar. I never went near the other door.

facts.fact: A clerk in grey with a desk at the winch-house, older than the grey cloaks and not one of them, gave him two wrapped things before the snow and had his sister's letter, written in the clerk's hand and signed with her private mark.
facts.evidence: He had a desk in the winch-house, they'd put a board on two kegs for him, and he had my sister's letter.

facts.fact: The clerk called the things a mercy for the wounded: the fever comes off a man through the floor if there is a stone to take it, as at the Spire; one under the hall, then the other under the far cots.
facts.evidence: He said the fever comes off a man through the floor if there's a stone to take it

facts.fact: He set the first by the wine stair with a trowel and a lamp and was sick on the stair; he never set the second.
facts.evidence: I set it and I came up and I was sick on the stair.

facts.fact: His sister Mirren went to the Spire at Calden to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, asked the wrong man in front of the wrong people, and is kept at Calden, comfortably, the clerk said twice.
facts.evidence: She went to the Spire to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, because they'd stopped, and she asked the wrong man, in front of the wrong people, and now she's—kept.

facts.fact: He never saw the clerk kneel; the grey cloaks all kneel at the dawn bell, and the clerk only wrote.
facts.evidence: "I never saw him kneel," Anselm said, to the floor.

facts.fact: He says the letters from Calden come up with the carter every seventh day, and there is always another letter.
facts.evidence: They come up with the carter

people.did: Came up behind Hollis's chair unheard, held out her hand for the second wrapped thing, closed her fingers on it, put it in her coat and said nothing more.
people.now: At the cot with the second wrapped thing in her coat beside the chip. She has said nothing to Darrow since the night of the lid but Give it here.

facts.fact: She took the second wrapped thing from the almoner's satchel into her coat without a word about it.
facts.evidence: she closed her fingers on it and looked at nothing, and put it in her coat, and said no more than that

codex.name: The wine stair
codex.text: A second way down to the undercroft: the old stair door where the House's wine was once laid down, below the kitchen end, opened by the almoner's stores key. Its stair comes out in the painted hall behind a pillar at the kitchen end, far from the iron-banded door and its flour. Brother Anselm carried the black sliver down it with a trowel and a lamp (Ch 4 Sc 1).

codex.name: Brother Anselm
codex.text: The House's almoner: a soft, tired lay brother in his forties with ink on two fingers, who keeps the stores and takes the letters down to the carter each week. Before the snow a clerk in grey at the winch-house gave him two wrapped things and called them a mercy for the wounded, with his sister's letter under his hand; he set one under the row by the wine stair and could not set the other. Hollis brought him to the Captain at dawn (Ch 4 Sc 1).

codex.name: Mirren
codex.text: Brother Anselm's sister, the brave one of the two by his account: she went to the Spire at Calden to ask what had become of the brothers' letters from Coldmere, asked the wrong man before the wrong people, and is kept at Calden, comfortably, a clerk said twice. Her letters to her brother come up the cage in the clerk's hand with her private mark under them (Ch 4 Sc 1).

fired.evidence: I counted the nights between. Two.
Brother. Tell the Captain what you told me at the third bell.
I say every name under this roof in this chapel every night, Captain, and I have not had to stop saying one since you came.

now.against: A clerk in grey at the winch-house who never kneels sent two black slivers up in the House's own satchel, and holds the almoner's sister at Calden; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the grey cloaks have their hand on the cage; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.
now.next: The next letter comes up with the carter.

title: Her Hand

where.detail: inside the wicket by the gate lamp at dusk, with Hollis in his chair, Wren, the almoner and Rae in the kitchen door

time: dusk, the day after the almoner's confession; the cage went down and came up empty
last_beat: Nobody answered him. The snow came in at the wicket and lay on the flags, and the almoner stood with his sister's hair inside his shirt and the stores key in his fist, and waited to be told.

people.did: Met Rae at the wicket; took the letter and knew its hand from the direction on his brother's letters; asked Rae twice where she had seen it and got only that she had; read Marrant's method whole: the lever, never the blade; heard the dealer holds the mare on his name till the thaw.
people.now: Inside the wicket at dusk with his hand open in the snow, having read the shape of Marrant's method; the almoner beside him waiting to be told what a captain does, and Hollis's question unanswered.

facts.fact: He knows the hand on the almoner's letter: the same upright clerk's hand with a long-tailed y that wrote the direction on all three of his brother's letters, and not Aldric's own.
facts.evidence: He had seen it three times on the outside of folded paper, over blue wax, addressed to the Captain of the Ninth

facts.fact: He believes Marrant's whole method is the lever and that he has never needed a blade: the almoner's sister squeezed with a lock of hair.
facts.evidence: He did not need a blade. He had never needed one. The lever was the whole of his method

facts.fact: He asked Rae twice where she had seen the hand and she would not say.
facts.evidence: "I've seen that hand," she said, to the door.

facts.fact: The feeling is coming back into the ends of his right-hand fingers under the linen as a dull red heat; the cold let go of him a little in the night.
facts.evidence: a dull red heat in the ends of the right one's fingers where the feeling was coming back under the linen

people.did: Came up the Steps at dusk with the almoner's letter inside her cloak rather than leave it in the cage overnight; put it in the Captain's hand, not the almoner's; would not say where she had seen the hand; from the kitchen door, told him the dealer took his name and holds the mare on it till the thaw.
people.now: In the kitchen door with a cup, counted in for the night. She has said she has seen that hand, and will not say where.

facts.fact: She carried the almoner's letter up the Steps herself rather than leave it in the cage overnight with the grey cloak's stool in the byre door.
facts.evidence: I'll not leave a thing like that in the cage overnight with that man's stool in the door.

facts.fact: She says she has seen the clerk's hand before, and will not say where.
facts.evidence: "I've seen it." Her shoulders did something under the cloak

facts.fact: The dealer on the Holloway took the Captain's name as surety: worth the mare's keep till the thaw and nothing past it; after the thaw it is coin or she is sold on.
facts.evidence: He said a captain's word was worth the mare's keep till the thaw, and nothing past it

people.did: Opened his sister's letter standing by the gate lamp; a lock of her dark hair fell from it; read it twice and did not weep; said the words are the clerk's and the mark is hers; said the clerk wrote it so that he would finish.
people.now: Inside the wicket with his sister's letter and her hair inside his shirt and the stores key in his fist, waiting to be told what the Captain will do with him.

facts.fact: His sister's letter says she is well kept, that he has a thing to finish, and that when it is finished he may fetch her home from Calden; it carries her private mark.
facts.evidence: She says they have told her I have a thing to finish, and that when it is finished I may come down to Calden and fetch her home.

facts.fact: He says his sister would never say she was well kept: the words are the clerk's, written for her to sign under.
facts.evidence: She'd never in her life say she was *well kept*. That's his word.

facts.fact: A lock of his sister's dark hair, tied with thread, came in the letter.
facts.evidence: A lock of hair. Dark, and tied with thread.

facts.fact: He did not weep; his face shut.
facts.evidence: The man's face had simply shut, like a door with no handle.

people.did: Had himself carried to the gate; asked, since nobody else would, what a captain does with a man who did a terrible thing for love.
people.now: In his chair inside the wicket with the lad's blanket on his knee, his question unanswered.

facts.fact: He asked what a captain does with a man who did a terrible thing for love, and nobody answered.
facts.evidence: What does a captain do with a man who did a terrible thing for love?

people.did: Saw Rae on the Last Hundred through Pell's glass with something held inside her cloak; ran to tell the Captain; caught the lock of hair before it reached the flags and gave it back.
people.now: Inside the wicket at dusk, having caught the lock of hair; she has no count for this.

facts.fact: She caught the lock of hair before it reached the flags.
facts.evidence: Wren caught it before it reached the flags.

codex.name: The letter from Calden
codex.text: A letter for Brother Anselm that Rae Thorne carried up the Steps rather than leave in the cage: addressed in a neat upright clerk's hand with a long-tailed y, the same hand that wrote the direction on the Captain's three letters from his brother. Inside, his sister's words as the clerk wrote them (she is well kept; he has a thing to finish; then he may fetch her home), her private mark under them, and a lock of her dark hair tied with thread (Ch 4 Sc 2).

fired.evidence: He said a captain's word was worth the mare's keep till the thaw, and nothing past it, and he'd hold her that long on it.

quest.name: The List
quest.on_the_page: The Confessors have come for the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's with a list: Darrow first, Hollis second. What stands between them and the hall is Old Mercy, the sanctuary bell: while it rings at dawn and dusk, no blade passes the gate and no name under it is taken down against its will. Marrant has not drawn a blade in a month. He has camped on the lower terrace, kept the cage, and reached into the House by the lever: a clerk in grey who never kneels sent two black slivers up in the House's own letter-satchel, one of them now set in the rock under the row and making the stone grow frost, and holds the almoner's sister at Calden for the second. Banners that are not grey are on the Holloway, a day off.

struggle: What a captain does with a good man who did a terrible thing for love, with the whole House watching him decide. The sliver stays in the wall under forty beds, one with the rock; the lid is off and whoever set it will know. Maelis has walked away from his telling and keeps two pieces of black glass in her coat. His fingertips are numb under the linen. The knee holds a stair at the Mender's count and no more, and the soft season is not over.

now.against: Marrant works the House by the lever, through a clerk's hand and a cage rope: the almoner's sister is held at Calden, and the clerk who never kneels writes her letters; one sliver is in the wall under the row, the other in Maelis's coat; the banners on the Holloway are a day off.
